content.title: March 10, 2026: Several Tornadoes in the Kankakee River Valley and Record Large Hail
content.text: Chicago, IL Weather Forecast Office Weather.gov > Chicago, IL > March 10, 2026: Several Tornadoes in the Kankakee River Valley and Record Large Hail Overview During the afternoon and evening of March 10, 2026, several intense supercell thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois and northwestern Indiana. ​A supercell is a thunderstorm that has persistent and deep rotation. One supercell was responsible for a family of 12 tornadoes across Livingston and Kankakee counties in Illinois, and Newton, Jasper, and Starke counties in northwestern Indiana. ​Information on the two tornadoes that were confirmed in Starke County, IN can be found on NWS Northern Indiana's summary web page for this event. A total of 10 tornadoes were confirmed in the NWS Chicago area of responsibility: An EF-0 tornado north of Pontiac, IL. An EF-U tornado near Cayuga, IL (midway between Pontiac and Odell). An EF-U tornado in Kankakee Township. This brief tornado occurred prior to the start of the Kankakee-Roselawn EF-3 tornado. An EF-U tornado in Otto Township. This brief tornado lifted just before the start of the Kankakee-Roselawn EF-3 tornado. An EF-3 tornado that tracked through southern Kankakee and Aroma Park in Illinois and Lake Village and Roselawn in Indiana before ending west of DeMotte, IN. An EF-1 satellite tornado just southwest of Sun River Terrace. This was a southward-moving satellite tornado associated with the Kankakee-Roselawn EF-3 tornado. An EF-U tornado immediately south of Sun River Terrace. This was a brief satellite tornado associated with the Kankakee-Roselawn EF-3 tornado. An EF-U tornado in southeastern Ganeer Township, southeast of Sun River Terrace. This was another brief satellite tornado associated with the Kankakee-Roselawn EF-3 tornado. An EF-U tornado in Momence Township, north of Hopkins Park. This was an anticyclonic satellite tornado that initially moved north, stopped, then tracked south before ending very near its starting location. An EF-1 tornado that tracked from southwest of Wheatfield to near Dunns Bridge, IN. A rare Level 4 out of 5 threat level for severe weather (driven by a relatively high probability for strong tornadoes) was issued by the Storm Prediction Center (SPC) prior to thunderstorms developing. A Tornado Watch was also issued before any of the tornadoes occurred and over 2 hours before the Kankakee - Roselawn tornado began. Based on preliminary reports, Tornado Warnings were also in effect before each tornado occurred. SPC Day One Convective Outlook issued at 11:28 AM CDT, which upgraded part of the area to a rare level 4/5 threat level for severe weather. SPC 11:28 AM CDT Day One Convective Outlook tornado probabilities, indicating a relatively high probability of strong tornadoes occurring south of I-80. SPC 11:28 AM CDT Day One Convective Outlook hail probabilities, indicating a relatively high probability of large hail occurring across most of the area. The Tornado Watch that was issued at 3:55 PM CDT. The Severe Thunderstorm Watch that was issued at 5:39 PM CDT. The supercell thunderstorms also produced exceptionally large hail. The same storm that produced all of the tornadoes in our area also produced hail that, during the height of the storm, ranged in size from 3 to locally 6 inches in diameter. Multiple hailstones with a diameter of 6" or greater were measured in Kankakee, IL. ​These hailstones are being considered for a new Illinois state largest hailstone record. The previous record was a hailstone measuring 4.75" in diameter that fell in Minooka in June of 2015. There is a process to verify the new record hailstone, so these 6+" hail reports are considered unofficial at this time. An announcement will be made in the coming weeks/months once the new record hailstone is confirmed. Once one of the 6+" diameter hailstones is officially confirmed as the new state record, that hailstone will also officially become the largest hailstone recorded east of the Mississippi River. Another supercell moved across the southern and western Chicago metropolitan area and dropped hail ranging in size from 2 to locally 4 inches in diameter across Bolingbrook, Woodridge, Downers Grove, Westmont, and Darien. The largest hailstone measured in this area was 4.8" in diameter and occurred in Darien, IL. Media use of NWS Web News Stories is encouraged!
